A.title: Spain RD 813/2026: Payment Ownership Checks for Operators
A.excerpt: Spain's new AML decree ties every deposit and withdrawal to the account holder. Existing players face a six-month remediation window.
body: Spain has turned payment-method ownership into a hard licensing condition for online gambling. Royal Decree 813/2026 of 7 October 2026, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 8 October (BOE-A-2026-20915), amends the regulation implementing Law 10/2010 on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing. Its new Article 21.2 requires licensed operators to confirm that the holder of the payment method used for deposits and withdrawals is the holder of the gaming account. The rule entered into force on 28 October 2026 and applies immediately to new players.

The significance lies in how far the obligation now reaches. A verified identity on the gaming account is no longer enough on its own. Every card, bank account and e-wallet that funds an account or receives winnings must be matched to the named player. Earlier policy discussion had contemplated this level of scrutiny only for players flagged as at risk; the decree applies it to the entire customer base. For compliance teams, that converts a targeted enhanced due diligence measure into a universal customer due diligence step.

Existing customers are given a transition period of six months, which industry calculations place at around 28 April 2027, although the BOE text itself does not state a calendar date. During that window players may continue to deposit and play, but they cannot withdraw winnings until their payment methods have been matched. Accounts that remain unmatched at the end of the period must be terminated, the DGOJ must be notified, and balances, including any withheld winnings, must be returned subject to AML and CFT obligations. Operators should document the basis on which they calculate the deadline, because the absence of a fixed date in the decree is likely to be tested in the first supervisory reviews.

The practical difficulty is that the decree prescribes the outcome but not the method. It does not specify which verification techniques are acceptable, and no detailed DGOJ or Sepblac guidance on the point had emerged at the time of writing. Remote identity procedures must meet the minimum requirements of Sepblac's general authorisations, and operators must keep records of the checks performed on initial transactions. In the absence of guidance, the defensible approach is a documented risk-based methodology: rely on account-holder name data returned by card schemes, open banking and e-wallet providers where available, and apply manual document review where it is not.

This places the payment stack squarely inside the KYC perimeter. Payment methods that cannot return verifiable holder data, such as some prepaid instruments and certain voucher products, now carry regulatory exposure, and operators should review whether they can continue to accept them as deposit channels. Contracts with payment service providers and processors should be revisited to secure the data fields needed, set service levels for name-match responses and allocate responsibility for failures. Where an e-wallet aggregates multiple underlying funding sources, operators will need to decide whether matching the wallet holder is sufficient or whether underlying instruments must also be checked.

The customer-facing risk is substantial. Players who have funded accounts with a partner's or relative's card will be unable to withdraw until they switch to an instrument in their own name, and withdrawal blocks are among the most common triggers for complaints and regulatory scrutiny. Operators should communicate the change well before the remediation deadline, explain clearly why winnings are being held, and ensure that complaint handling and safer gambling teams are equipped to deal with the inevitable volume. Withheld balances must be ring-fenced and returned in a way that is itself consistent with AML obligations, which may require additional source-of-funds checks for large sums.

For boards and compliance officers, the immediate priorities are a gap analysis of the current payment estate, a remediation plan for the existing player base with milestones before April 2027, updated AML policies and manuals reflecting new Article 21.2, and a record of the verification logic chosen and why. Given the overlap with Spain's existing restrictions on advertising and bonusing, and continuing debate over cross-operator deposit limits, operators should expect the DGOJ to treat payment-ownership failures as a priority inspection item once the transition closes. Specialist advisers in Spain can help align technical change with the legal timetable and engage with the regulator where guidance remains unclear.

A.title: Italy's New Remote Gaming System Delayed to February 2027
A.excerpt: ADM has split the switchover into phased certification deadlines ending 15 February 2027. What concessionaires and suppliers must deliver.
body: Italy's Customs and Monopolies Agency (ADM) has reset the timetable for the technical migration that underpins the new generation of online gaming concessions. Rather than a single conformity deadline, ADM has adopted a phased schedule: concessionaire service providers whose systems are offered to other concessionaires must upload their compliance-check results by 13 November 2026, concessionaires relying on those third-party systems must do so by 13 January 2027, technical-functional verifications must be completed by 12 February 2027, and the new concessionaire system goes into production on 15 February 2027. ADM has publicly cited operational difficulties and a low volume of certification requests as reasons for moving the start date.

The phased approach reflects the technical dependencies in the certification chain. Each block of activity is a precondition for the next: provider platforms must be certified before the operators that build on them, and components that populate the shared library must be certified before game-level testing can proceed. Technical-functional verifications must be completed for each vertical, including sports betting, casino, virtual events, skill games, poker, horse racing, bingo and Totocalcio. A delay at the supplier level therefore cascades directly into the concessionaire's own compliance position.

ADM has also eased some parallel obligations while the migration runs. By note prot. 666678 of 16 October 2026, it exempted gaming platforms from periodic compliance checks for the first half of 2027. In a clarifying note, prot. 700357 of 10 November 2026, it confirmed that for authorisation titles already issued, concessionaires need not renew certifications falling due between 1 October and 31 December 2026. Both notes are expressly without prejudice to other certification and verification obligations, so operators should not read them as a general suspension of technical compliance.

For concessionaires, the legal risk is that formal compliance with deadlines will not be enough if certifications are incomplete at switchover. Industry participants have warned that an uncertified offer on 15 February 2027 could shrink the legal market, with consequences for gaming volumes, tax revenue and channelisation towards unauthorised sites. Concessionaires should treat the dates as hard regulatory milestones and assume that products not certified by the production date may need to be withdrawn from the Italian market until they are.

Supplier contracts are the critical pressure point. Concessionaires that depend on a third-party system cannot meet the 13 January 2027 deadline unless their provider meets the 13 November 2026 deadline, yet many platform agreements were negotiated before the new concession framework was finalised. Operators should check whether their contracts contain specific obligations to achieve Italian certification by fixed dates, what remedies apply if a supplier misses them, and whether the concessionaire has audit and information rights over the provider's certification status. Where these protections are weak, a contractual side letter now is far cheaper than a dispute after a failed launch.

Verification bodies are also a bottleneck. With many operators and suppliers seeking testing in the same window, capacity at accredited laboratories may be limited, and the 12 February deadline for technical-functional verifications leaves little room for retesting. Concessionaires should book testing capacity early, prioritise their highest-revenue verticals and prepare fallback plans for products that may not be ready. Trade bodies have asked for further dialogue with ADM, and it is possible that additional practical guidance will follow, but operators should not plan on another postponement.

The migration sits alongside other changes in the Italian regime, including the new concession fees and the consolidation of brands under single licences, and ADM's continuing blacklist enforcement against unlicensed domains. Taken together, they make the first quarter of 2027 a period of concentrated regulatory risk for the Italian market. Italian gaming counsel can assist with mapping obligations against the ADM calendar, reviewing supplier arrangements and managing correspondence with the Agency where certification issues arise.

A.title: Florida Regulator Pushes Felony Penalties for Illegal Slots
A.excerpt: After SB 1580 died in March, the FGCC wants tougher slot penalties in 2027. What it means for sweepstakes and offshore operators.
body: Florida's gaming regulator has signalled that illegal gambling will be a priority in the 2027 legislative session. On 9 November 2026, Alana Zimmer, executive director of the Florida Gaming Control Commission (FGCC), said the current misdemeanour charge for hosting illegal slot machines is too weak to deter repeat offenders. She pointed to new operations opening soon after closures, cases being dismissed, and prosecutors prioritising more serious crimes. Attorney General James Uthmeier has also pressed lawmakers for tougher penalties.

Under section 849.23 of the Florida Statutes, a first slot-machine conviction is a second-degree misdemeanour, a second is a first-degree misdemeanour, and only a third violation after two prior convictions becomes a third-degree felony. The FGCC's own enforcement figures illustrate why the agency considers this inadequate: it reported seizing 6,725 illegal slot machines and $14,474,336 in 2025, compared with 1,287 machines and $7,110,613 in 2024. Seizures at that scale, combined with low-level charges, suggest that operators treat enforcement as a cost of doing business.

The legislative vehicle for reform already exists. CS/CS/SB 1580, titled Illegal Gaming, passed the Senate 34-0 on 6 March 2026 and the House 82-31 on 11 March 2026, but died in returning messages in the Senate on 13 March 2026 without reaching the governor. The bill would have made trafficking in slot machines a first-degree felony and, significantly for the online sector, would have defined internet gambling and internet sports wagering so that online activity fell expressly within the same statute. Related bills, HB 189, HB 591 and SB 1164, also failed. With broad support in both chambers, a revived version is a realistic prospect.

The timetable is short. The Legislature holds its organisation session on 17 November 2026, interim committee weeks run from 30 November 2026 through February 2027, and the 2027 regular session convenes on 2 March and is scheduled to end on 30 April 2027. Businesses with exposure to Florida should expect a bill to be filed during interim committee weeks and should engage early, because definitional language, not headline penalty levels, will determine who is caught.

The definitions are where the real risk lies for online operators. Florida's Attorney General filed suits on 19 August 2026 in Hillsborough County Circuit Court against Stake and VGW, the operator of Chumba Casino, LuckyLand and Global Poker, together with their payment processors, alleging illegal online gambling and violations of the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and seeking injunctions, forfeiture, restitution and civil penalties. A statute that expressly defines internet gambling would strengthen the state's hand in such litigation and could expose payment processors, affiliates and suppliers to criminal liability as well as civil claims.

Sports wagering adds a further layer. Under the 2021 compact, Hard Rock Bets is the only online sportsbook with legal status in Florida, and the Seminole Tribe has sued DraftKings in Broward Circuit Court alleging it operates an illegal sportsbook in breach of the Tribe's exclusivity. Zimmer has also noted that prediction market platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket remain active in the state, and that she expects the US Supreme Court to resolve whether such platforms are exchanges or sportsbooks. Any new statutory definition of internet sports wagering will be drafted with these disputes in mind.

Operators of sweepstakes casinos, offshore sites and adjacent services should treat the coming session as a material risk event. Practical steps include reviewing Florida customer exposure and geolocation controls, auditing payment and affiliate relationships for the state, preserving documents relevant to existing litigation, and preparing written submissions on proposed definitions. Land-based route operators and amusement game businesses should also check whether their machines could be caught by broader trafficking provisions. Florida gaming counsel can advise on legislative engagement and on structuring operations to reduce exposure before any new law takes effect.

A.title: Nebraska Rejects Online Sports Betting: 2027 State Outlook
A.excerpt: Voters defeated Initiatives 440 and 441 by about ten points. Where the midterm results leave US sports betting and iGaming expansion.
body: Nebraska voters have rejected online sports betting. In the 3 November 2026 election, Initiative 440, a constitutional amendment to authorise online sports wagering, was defeated by roughly 55% to 45%, and Initiative 441, the companion measure setting a regulatory framework and tax structure for mobile wagering, failed 54.5% to 45.5% on unofficial returns pending certification by the Secretary of State. Mobile and online sports betting therefore remain illegal statewide, while in-person wagering at licensed racetrack casinos, approved by voters in 2020, continues.

The result is notable because of the resources behind the campaign. Tax Relief Nebraska, a coalition backed by the state's casinos and online sports betting interests, spent more than $22 million and turned to the ballot after years of resistance in the Legislature. Its central pitch was that legalisation would capture revenue from Nebraskans already betting illegally or across state lines and direct it to property tax relief. Opponents, including Gambling with the Good Life, the Open Door Mission and the Nebraska Family Alliance, focused on youth and student-athlete harm and questioned whether meaningful tax relief would follow. Senator Pete Ricketts, re-elected on the same ballot, publicly criticised the tax-relief claims.

The lesson for operators is that the revenue argument, which has carried most state legalisation debates since 2018, is losing persuasive force with voters. Public concern about mobile access, advertising intensity and young adults is now a mainstream political issue, and opponents can win with far smaller budgets. Future ballot campaigns are likely to need stronger, more concrete responsible gambling commitments, such as advertising restrictions, deposit limit tools and dedicated problem gambling funding, if they are to succeed.

Elsewhere, the midterms shifted the political landscape in ways that may open doors in 2027. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship and Democrats flipped the House for the first time since 2004, while Republicans held the Senate 29-27; Bottoms has supported a constitutional amendment to legalise casinos. Any Georgia expansion still requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers before going to voters, and a sports betting amendment fell short in the House earlier in 2026. In Ohio, Governor-elect Amy Acton supported online casino legalisation during her campaign and could include it in the biennial budget, although Republicans retain both chambers.

Minnesota's expanded DFL majorities, with a 39-28 Senate and a 77-57 House, may help revive the long-stalled tribal, charity and racetrack sports betting compromise, particularly if sports betting advocate Rep. Zack Stephenson becomes House speaker. In South Carolina, Governor-elect Alan Wilson supports online sports betting with safeguards but has pledged to veto casino legislation. Alabama's Governor-elect Tommy Tuberville has said he will not block expansion but wants a comprehensive plan, and with constitutional amendments requiring three-fifths approval, November 2028 is the earliest realistic voter opportunity. In Oklahoma, a change of governor may reopen tribal compact discussions after an April 2026 sports betting bill failed in the Senate.

For iGaming, the 2027 map remains incremental. Illinois has seen online casinos proposed for revenue, Indiana considered an iGaming bill in 2026 without a floor vote, Massachusetts referred an online casino bill for study, and Virginia made progress that sets up another attempt. In New York, Senator Joseph Addabbo continues to introduce online casino bills against labour and land-based casino opposition. Texas would require voter approval and, as analysts have warned, any measure there would face heavily funded opposition.

Operators planning US market entry should therefore build 2027 strategies around legislatures rather than ballots, and around states where governors have expressly signalled support. Early engagement with tribal stakeholders in compact states, credible responsible gambling packages and realistic tax proposals will matter more than headline revenue estimates. US gaming counsel can help prioritise target states, monitor bill filings as sessions open in January and February, and prepare licensing applications so that operators are ready to move once enabling legislation passes.

A.title: South Africa's 20% Online Gambling Levy: February Decision
A.excerpt: Treasury's national levy on online GGR survived the October MTBPS. Operators face a possible 38-39% effective rate from 2027.
body: South Africa's proposed national tax on online gambling is moving towards a decision. National Treasury's discussion paper, The Case for a National Online Gambling Tax, published on 25 November 2025, proposed a 20% levy on the gross gambling revenue of online betting and interactive gambling operators, charged in addition to existing taxes and framed as a sin tax comparable to excise on alcohol and tobacco. The Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement of 21 October 2026 kept the proposal alive without confirming a rate or start date, and the final design is now expected in the February 2027 Budget, followed by draft legislation and a further round of public comment. The tax is not yet in force.

Treasury's rationale rests on the scale and growth of the market. Around R1.5 trillion was wagered in 2024/25, with gross gambling revenue of R74.5 billion, and online betting now accounts for more than 85% of betting GGR. Treasury estimates that the levy would raise more than R10 billion a year. Public comment closed on 27 February 2026 after two extensions, and Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana has said that submissions generally recognised the need to address the growth and harms of online gambling.

The central legal and commercial question is how the levy interacts with existing provincial taxation. Provinces currently tax online betting at roughly 6% to 9% of GGR, and bookmakers also account for VAT, giving an estimated combined burden of 18% to 19%. A national 20% levy layered on top would lift the effective rate to around 38% to 39%. Whether the national levy will replace, offset or sit alongside provincial taxes remains open, and because gambling is a concurrent national and provincial competence under the Constitution, the answer has implications for intergovernmental relations as well as for operators.

Industry bodies have raised structural objections. The South African Responsible Operators Gambling Association (SAROGA) argues that a national levy would change the regulatory settlement through tax rather than through legislation, effectively allowing national policy to reshape a provincially licensed market without the scrutiny that a gambling statute would receive. Licensed operators also warn that a heavy levy could push bettors towards unlicensed offshore sites that pay no South African tax and offer fewer consumer protections, undermining both revenue and harm-reduction goals.

A further complication is the treatment of online casino. Treasury's paper proposes taxing online casino revenue even though interactive casino gaming remains unlawful at national level. Taxing an activity that the law prohibits raises questions of legal coherence and could be read as a signal that national legalisation of online casino is being contemplated. Operators and suppliers should not treat the proposal as legalisation, however; until the regulatory framework changes, offering online casino to South African players remains a criminal and licensing risk.

For operators, the practical exposure is to margins and product design. A combined effective rate near 39% of GGR would place South Africa among the higher-taxed betting markets globally and would put pressure on bonusing, odds margins and marketing spend. Group finance teams should model scenarios with and without provincial offset, assess the effect on licensed versus offshore pricing, and consider how the tax base will be defined, including treatment of free bets, promotional credits and bets placed on foreign events. Transitional provisions and the effective date will also matter for contracts with affiliates and suppliers that are priced on revenue share.

The window to influence the outcome is now. Between the MTBPS and the February 2027 Budget, Treasury will be finalising design choices, and the subsequent draft legislation will give a further opportunity to comment. Operators should prepare evidence on channelisation, offshore leakage and the cumulative tax burden, coordinate positions through industry associations, and engage with both national and provincial authorities. Advisers with South African gaming and tax experience can help structure submissions and plan for the range of outcomes the Budget may bring.
